title: Task scheduler class diagram
idea: The class design splits a scheduler into a `Task` that holds state, a `Job` that holds the work, and small interfaces for timing, retries and the clock.

analogy.text: A hospital ward board. Each card names a patient, a time and an urgency. The nurse reads the board; the doctor does the work.
analogy.breaks: Cards never fail and come back; tasks do, with a later time.

points: `Scheduler` owns the queue and offers submit, cancel and run-due.
`Task` holds run time, priority, attempts and a status with guarded moves.
`Schedule` says when to run again; `RetryPolicy` sets the wait after a failure.
A `Clock` interface replaces the system clock, so tests control time.

edges.label: has many
edges.caption: The scheduler keeps tasks in a priority queue ordered by run time, then priority, then submit order.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: Every status change goes through one method that refuses illegal moves.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: The task holds the job but never knows what the job does.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: After a success, the schedule answers when the task runs again, or never.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: After a failure, the retry policy answers whether to try again and after what delay.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: The scheduler asks the injected clock for now. Tests pass a manual clock.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: FixedRate and OneShot implement Schedule. New schedules plug in without edits to the scheduler.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: ExponentialBackoff implements RetryPolicy. New retry policies plug in the same way.

code.title: The Java model
code.caption: The model with its invariants: queue order, a guarded state machine, and exponential backoff with a cap.

walk.text: Three tasks enter a PriorityQueue that uses the task ordering rule.
Polling returns them in run order, not insertion order.
Four small interfaces: work, time, repeat and retry.
The status enum lists which moves are legal from each state.
Order by run time, then higher priority, then submit sequence.
Only requeueAt changes the run time, and every move is checked.
Backoff doubles per attempt, capped, with the shift bounded.

pitfalls: Do not let the scheduler know job details; it only calls run and catches failures.
Never change a task's run time while it sits inside the priority queue.
Add a submit sequence to the comparator, or equal tasks come out in arbitrary order.

quiz.q: What does the backoff line of ClassDesign print?
quiz.why: Attempt 1 waits the base 100 ms; each later attempt doubles it. The fifth would be 1600, but the cap holds it at 1000.

takeaway: Task holds state, Job holds work, interfaces hold every policy.

starters: Why is Job separate from Task instead of Task having a run method?
Should TaskStatus be on Task or kept inside the Scheduler?
